utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've expressed my apologies privately. I wonder if I could simply say that I am sorry that I was the cause of the lateness in court this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Stewart. Ms. Hanson, first of all, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and I was informed that you had, perhaps, an answer to one or two of our questions. Perhaps, Mr. Hannis, we should give we should give Ms. Hanson an opportunity to give those answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. You had inquired about document P0008404 through P0008410. It's a report on the list of motor vehicles at the logistics base in Cirkin Polje. That document had been brought to my attention by Ewen Brown, who had written a report on the military. Mr. Brown is no longer at the Tribunal, but I consulted his report to see if he had more information about this document. And what I see is he actually uses the next document -- a related document which appears right next to it in the evidence, P0008411 through P0008420, which is a related document, similarly from the logistics base of the Crisis Staff in Cirkin Polje, dated the 16th of September, 1992. I have a copy, and a copy of the translation, if it's of interest to you. I noted it had been disclosed in this case on the 14th of December last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a copy for the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have two copies. One has been highlighted. I was just going to read the highlighted portion. I'm sorry. I don't have three copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we -- if one of the copies could be put on the ELMO, and then the other copy be given to Mr. Stewart, and then perhaps you could read, Ms. Hanson, the portion you thought relevant. I'm afraid I forgot what the tab number was of the Cirkin Polje, and it might be that -- because the long numbers, I can't memorise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it's 178, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 178. And it certainly will be in the binder that's on my desk downstairs. Yes, it starts with 179. Perhaps you can read it and we'll check it later on the basis of the material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, this was dated on the 16th of September, and it discusses in the first paragraph the setting up of the logistics base, and in the second paragraph, the fact that it distributed meals to army and police and prisoners in Omarska, Keraterm, and refugees in Trnopolje. And it says that a report about the distribution of food had been given to the Crisis Staff, the police, public security station, and a copy of the report kept for the base's files. This report also makes reference on the last page that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reporting, therefore, was mainly at the local level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Simply, there's a reference on the last page that they attach the list of motor vehicles from the logistics base of Cirkin Polje, dated the 17th of June, 1992. And since these two documents were found together, they appear next to each other in the evidence record, they both indicate that they were found in the municipal building in Prijedor. I take it that they were presented together. They were found among materials of the Prijedor executive committee, dating from October 1992, and the minutes from that session indicate that they discussed the work of the logistics base in Cirkin Polje. So I take it these material -- it would be logical that these materials were together because they were being examined at the time by the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, we have no indication that this material went higher up in the hierarchy than the Prijedor level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No indication of that in these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I wonder whether, Mr. Hannis, whether it's necessary to include this document in evidence. It rather confirms that it was reporting on the municipality level rather than ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm willing to stipulate that with Mr. Stewart, or we can have this marked as an additional exhibit, whichever the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment at least, the Chamber ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no specific wish of the Chamber to receive that additional document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Examined by Mr. Hannis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, when we left off yesterday we were talking about the treatment or the status of the non-Serbs in the municipalities vis-a-vis the Crisis Staffs. I'm ready now to have you take a look at presentation tab 203, which is master tab number 312, and we'll follow the same procedure we've been doing of putting the B/C/S up in Sanction and the English on the ELMO. And if you would direct us to the excerpt you wanted to discuss. This is from the Sipovo municipality Crisis Staff meeting on the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it's page 3 in the translation. I'm just going to find it in the original. Yes, it's at the top of 02194122 in the B/C/S, the very top line, and on page 3 in the English, indicating that the Crisis Staff is discussing whether Muslims will live here in Sipovo, and that they should -- whether the Crisis Staff should take a stand with regard to Muslims. So it was, once again, an issue. One of the topics of discussion, for Crisis Staffs was the status of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you presentation tab 204, master tab 311, from the Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the Crisis Staff of Pale, dated the 7th of May, 1992, ordering the -- that the following telephone numbers be disconnected. All of these names on this list appear to be Muslim names. And the last item, or last remark on the top of the second page, that 10 of those 15 numbers are to be given to Serbian Television Pale. It's a small detail, but it indicates the kind of business with which Crisis Staffs were occupied and the kind of measures they could take against Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would like to recall to you that our crime-base witness from Pale testified about this document, and one of the names on that list was his neighbour. Next, we're going to skip tabs 205 and 206, Your Honours and counsel. These are referred to in footnotes in Ms. Hanson's report. And I want to go to tab 207, master tab 322.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document from the Vogosca Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the conclusions of the Vogosca Crisis Staff, dated the 17th of May, 1992. Under item 5, you would note that they are laying off specifically Muslim and Croat staff from the hospital. This is also an interesting document for a few other themes I've mentioned, if I could briefly point out. Item number 1, it's saying that they are -- the Crisis Staff will issue an order for taking over the army barracks which are being placed under the command of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Assembly of Vogosca, which is under the sole command of the Serb Republic of BiH. If you'll note the date, the 17th of May, following the establishment of the VRS, they're now asserting their control -- authority over the army barracks, and it gives an indication of hierarchy. The barracks are under the command of the Crisis Staff, which is under the command of the Serb Republic. Also, item 2, discussing the cleansing, ciscenje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Excuse me. In that 207, what does it mean that number 2, "for the 'cleansing' of Svrake and other territories, one more man is to be secured, apart from Mr. Borovcanin." What's the meaning of it, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the word cleansing, ciscenje, has a variety of meanings, and it's not sufficiently clear from this sentence alone whether they mean the military term of clearing the terrain after a battle or mopping up the last resistance or the way we see it used in many other cases as -- also known as ethnic cleansing. I would note in this case that Svrake was a predominantly Muslim settlement, over 80 per cent Muslim. And I see that, in fact, the revised translation didn't get into my binder, so perhaps if we put up Mr. Hannis's translation, a little bit of the confusion is removed because -- no, it didn't get revised. I'm sorry, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the computer -- under the computer evidence button, you'll find the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have the original here. I would just note that the second sentence refers to the cleansing not of Svrake as it appears in the translation but Semizovac, and if the interpreters can confirm that's a reference to Semizovac not Svrake. So the first sentence, they're talking about cleansing Svrake, getting one more person for that. The second sentence, they're saying when to cleanse Semizovac in the case of firing, any shooting. What precisely they mean here by cleansing, this document alone doesn't give an indication of what kind of cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I observe, it's extremely helpful - I don't suggest it's not helpful for Ms. Hanson to give an explanation and go as far as she can - I can also observe that actually Ms. Hanson's use of mopping up is entirely consistent with the discussion we had some weeks ago on that precise phrase. So I am certainly not quarrelling with Ms. Hanson about that. But clearly, Your Honour, if we do get to points where it does become important to resolve meanings of words and translations, we have to go beyond this particular witness whose expertise lies in other areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But whenever a word appears that comes even close to cleaning, cleansing, mopping, whatever, the Chamber will be immediately alert on the proper meaning of those words. I'm not saying that I'm waking up at night and considering all these different sensations, but it comes close to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour. But thank you for that observation, Your Honour. We appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, I know in this case, cleansing is actually in quotation marks in the original, no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is unusual. Again, on the basis of one sentence, I can't speculate as to why it is. But it's unusual to see it in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, I think, in your report you talked about how Crisis Staffs exercise some control over the freedom of movement within the municipalities. Tabs 208 and 209, Your Honours, I want to skip over. They're referred to in the footnotes in her report, and go to tab 210, which is master tab 326, and ask you to comment on this one, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision of the Crisis Staff of Ilidza municipality, dated the 19th of May, 1992, signed by Nedeljko Prstojevic as commander of the Crisis Staff, prohibiting the moving out of Croats and Muslims from Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica, and stating that no passage is allowed from the direction of Sarajevo without a special written approval of the Crisis Staff. In this connection, you might remember the intercepted conversation dated the 23rd of May, between Prstojevic and Gagovic, saying that he had set such a policy that no one can come out from Sarajevo. If you'll note that this -- in the distribution of this, it says, number 1, all Crisis Staffs. I would note here what I have noted in my report, that in some municipalities, there was also -- there were also Crisis Staffs at the lower -- the next lower level, the local community level. And we have seen such in Ilidza. I would take this to mean that all of the local level Crisis Staffs, the local community Crisis Staffs, not all Crisis Staffs in Bosnia, because it doesn't seem logical there. That's my interpretation of that particular notation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hanson, in addition to controlling freedom of movement, in your report, I think you next discuss how the Crisis Staffs established a local judicial system and appointed Serbs to judgeships and prosecutorships and removed non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw mention of that in Rajko Dukic's speech in the Assembly in July 1992, and we have many documents that indicate that power of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next two, Your Honours, tab 211 and 212, I'll will skip over. They're in her report, in the footnotes. But I would like to go to tab 213 in the presentation, which is master tab number 423.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is from Doboj. I'd ask you to comment on this one for us, please.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's perhaps a little clearer in the original, because it's all on one page, but this is a letter from the president of the Serbian municipality of Doboj, also signed by the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, dated the 24th of June, 1992, addressed to the Ministry of Justice of the Serbian Republic. I would note that this document was found in the archives of the Ministry of Justice. And the notations on it show -- there's a handwritten notation saying it's implemented, done, yes. It's a recommendation for the appointment of public prosecutors in Doboj, and if I could see that -- yes. It's proposing the leaving -- dismissal of three public prosecutors. Their names, I note -- the first two names are Muslim and the third name Ante, son of Stipe, would be typically a Croatian name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the handwritten notations there also say they've been relieved. So it's an indication that the non-Serbs were dismissed and -- I'm sorry, that the proposal -- that it was proposed that non-Serbs be dismissed and Serbs appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following on from that, I'd like to show you presentation tab 214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Before these events, before this took place, how were prosecutors appointed? Were municipalities -- did municipalities intervene in the appointment of prosecutors? Do we have any information about that? Does that mean that this is a completely new practice that has nothing to do with what was done in the past, with the rules that applied in the past in the republic? Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I draw attention to the fact that in the -- I'm looking at tab 213, that the English translation, where it says that -- bottom of page 2, "handwritten and double-underlined relieved," indicates that the word "relieved" is in translation is handwritten and double-underlined. What it doesn't indicate, but it's very clear on the original B/C/S version, is that those three names are crossed out, Midhat Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon me. Yes, I am not familiar with the earlier proceedings, but in general, what I know of the relationship between the authorities of the municipal assembly and those of a higher level, I think it would be much -- a similar practice that the municipal proposes the candidates and the ministry approves or not, generally, approving. But I can't say that with complete confidence. I understand -- I am not claiming here that this is a new power, but rather I am looking at how the Crisis Staff used that power. That's the focus of my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness appears to be treating my observation as a question. It was purely an observation, and it seems in relation also to one or two other items on this document, that a little bit of care is needed to make sure that the particular items in the translation -- it is seen how they match the items in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, would it be possible to have an English translation? Because there's no problem with the translation, as such, as far as I understand, but that all other handwriting, crossing out, is reflected in the English translation and -- well, I understood Ms. Hanson's answer to be that since Judge Hanoteau first put a question, which was not directly related to your observation, rather rightly, that she first answered the question of Judge Hanoteau, and I think we dealt with the other matter by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That may be what happened. I see that now, Your Honour. I just thought that somebody might have made a comment in response to my comment. Anyway, never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then following on that decision, I wanted to show you presentation tab 214, master tab 423, which appears to relate.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It relates -- it is the decision on appointing the public prosecutors in Doboj, signed by Radovan Karadzic as president of the Presidency. And it is the -- the three names, Serbian names, proposed in the previous document. So we had the handwritten annotation that that decision had been -- that proposal had been done, and this is the -- an official decision indicating that it had been acted on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I want to go to presentation tab 215, and the master tab number is 424. This is from Banja Luka, and deals with the same issue. Can you tell us what this one shows?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interesting document because it shows the process of the proposal of -- and confirmation of appointments of some judicial offices, in this case, in Banja Luka. The first page is the cover letter from the public prosecutors' office in Banja Luka to the War Presidency of the Banja Luka municipal assembly, stating that the War Presidency must give its approval for the appointment of the deputy public prosecutor. So they are forwarding to the War Presidency for its approval a list of candidates for the office of public prosecutors. If we look at the list on the following pages, following three pages in the translation - in the B/C/S, it's two pages, 03234587 through 03234588 - if we can see the originals -- in the originals, it's quite striking that it's noted in the translation that all the names are circled except the last name - I'm just looking at the original to confirm it - which is a Muslim name. We can tell who is a Muslim and Serb because that is noted for each name, and it is underlined in handwriting. So there are handwritten annotations circling the numbers and underlining nationalities. The only name that is crossed out is the last Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information for the Court where this particular document was obtained from?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was found in the archives of the Ministry of Justice, so it indicates that this was forwarded from the public prosecutors' office to the War Presidency, and got from the War Presidency of Banja Luka municipality to the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see another document later on actually reflecting what might have been taken in connection with these proposals?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me hand you a document, which is tab number 216, master tab 425, and you to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, may I ask for a clarification on the previous answer. Ms. Hanson, you said only the last name was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are two lists, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first is the shorter list of candidates for public prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the second list, which we'll get to in a moment, is for judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I went too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we're jumping ahead to the next document because it relates only to the first list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which candidates were those, judges or prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutors. So the first list of prosecutors, the next document that you see, it's the decision on appointing deputy public prosecutors in Banja Luka, signed by Momcilo Krajisnik as president of the Assembly, dated the 11th of August. And that list -- the appointments here correspond to the Serb names on that list of proposed candidates, and the Muslim name is not appointed, which had been X-ed out on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you refer us to the B/C/S ERN?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the decision? I'm sorry. Of the decision?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It is 03234584 through 03234585.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last name that was on the list in the previous document among prosecutor candidates was the Muslim name?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that person was not appointed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a question, a very brief question? I'm somewhat confused, I'm somewhat lost, with these lists, and I would like to get an explanation. I'm still with tab 215. We have a first list of names under our eyes here, and this first list of names has 11 names. You told us that the last name was a Muslim name, that this name was a Muslim name. That's the eleventh name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the following list, what does it represent? We have the second list. We can see that there are 50 names on this second list. Some numbers are circled and other numbers are crossed out, or there's a cross over them. You explained this to us, but I didn't really quite understand. Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, if I can show the original, because it's not in Cyrillic, it might be quite clear. The second list, the longer list, is candidates for judge, so it's separate -- it's not -- it's a separate list from the first list. For the first list, we have the decision on appointments; for this one, we do not. But if you look at the original, for each name, the nationality is underlined, and each name that is underlined is Serb there in the original, Srpkinja or Srbinje is circled. Each name that is not a Serb nationality is crossed out. On the first page of the list, that's 03234589, you can see the first crossed-out name, the nationality Hrvatica, means Croatian. Numbers 8 and 9 -- okay, number 8 is Srpkinja, is a Serb, but I would note that her father is identified as Avdo and the last name is Fazlic -- sorry, her married name is Fazlic. The Avdo would be a typically Muslim name. She identifies herself as Serb, and her name is crossed out. But Fazlic also is more usually a Muslim last name, although that is harder to judge. That is one of the exceptions of a Serb being crossed out. The next name that's crossed out is, in fact, Muslim. The next page, the name that's crossed out, number 14, is Croat. Number 19, crossed out, Yugoslav; 20, Yugoslav, crossed out; 24, Slovene, crossed out; 25, Muslim, crossed out; 26, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Muslim, crossed out; 29, Yugoslav, crossed, and so on. There are a few Serb names that are crossed out, but there is an explanation following this list that refugees cannot be employed, and the indication is that these are -- the indication from where they worked before, that they are not from Banja Luka, and it is my opinion that it's likely that they were refugees and therefore names were crossed out as not suitable. But it is notable that nobody identified as a Muslim or Croat has their name circled. Somebody marked up this list, it's clear, and identified the nationality by underlining, in addition to naming it when they drew up the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I now wanted to move on to another topic. In your report, at paragraph 61, you talk about how Crisis Staffs carried out a policy and procedures for the removal or forcible departure of non-Serbs. I'd like you to take a look at tab 217 in the presentation, that's master tab 141. This is a Crisis Staff decision from the 30th of May, 1992, from Sanski Most. It's a document we've seen before on another topic, but could you tell us how it pertains to this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under item 2, at the bottom of the first page in translation, the second paragraph on the second page of the B/C/S, 00471744, notes that the Crisis Staff needs to find a long-term solution for Muslims and Croats who are not loyal to the constitution and laws of the Serbian Republic of BiH, which means that all those who've not taken up arms and want to change their municipality are to be allowed to move away. The Crisis Staff also notes that they should make contact with the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding implementation on the idea of resettlement of the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I would like to show you presentation tab 218, master tab 426. This is from Bosanski Novi Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an announcement of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi, dated the 8th of June, addressed to the citizens of Blagaj and the Japra valley, saying that in regard to the war operations and a decision -- information from the Red Cross of Bosanski Novi about the departure of Muslims -- the problem of the departure of Muslims, the Crisis Staff here advises the citizens that they are prepared to provide peaceful and secure departure of the Muslim population from that area. "With a view to your security, it is necessary to form a departure column immediately. If these proposals are rejected, the Crisis Staff will no longer be able to guarantee security for Muslims in this area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would recall you to the testimony of a couple of crime-base witnesses from Bosanski Novi about how they came to be moved out of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, Ms. Hanson, I would ask you to look at presentation tab 219, master tab 295. This is from, I think, a document that we looked at other portions of before, and I think the excerpt you want to talk about here is on page 10 of the English translation. Can you direct Mr. Krajisnik to the appropriate place in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it's on page 12 of the document, B0032538, the last full paragraph from the bottom of that page. It notes that 3.500 Muslims from the Japra valley came to an agreement with the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, and on the 9th of June, left the municipality in the direction of Doboj. The previous document was dated the 8th of June. "This resettlement was done by rail in a train composed of 22 wagons. The SJB has no precise data because these citizens did not officially unregister their residents in accordance with the law." I take that is a confirmation related to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go on to another municipality. Presentation tab 220, master tab 427. This is from the Gacko municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a proclamation of the War Presidency of Gacko, dated the 31st of July, 1992, a proclamation to the Muslim people in Bileca, telling them to come down out of -- where they had sought refuge in the mountains, saying -- I take attention to item 3 on the list, bottom of the first page of the translation; in the B/C/S, on the second page, 02096314, item 3 on the first -- on the top of the page. "After leaving the mountains, you will immediately be put on buses. The women, children and the elderly will be taken where they wish to go, while the men fit for military service will be taken to the garrison prison in Bileca." And item 5 on the next page in the translation: "The possible destinations are Stolac, Mostar, and Macedonia. There are no other possibilities due to the present circumstances." So although they say that they may go -- be sent where they wish to go, in fact their only choices are in either territory held by the Bosnian and Croat forces -- Muslim and Croat forces in Bosnia or Macedonia, another country altogether. And the men, of course, will be sent to the prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to show you tab 221, master tab number 13. This is from the Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a decision of the Crisis Staff, dated the 22nd of June, 1992, "a decision on the organised moving out of refugees disloyal to the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Under Article 1, it says: "All refugees who are disloyal to the authorities, as well as refugees whose relatives are members of enemy formations, are obliged to leave Prnjavor in an organised fashion." And it tasks the police station, the public security station, to implement this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me show you tab 222, master tab number 221. This is from the Bosanska Krupa municipality, although in connection with that I see there's a different name on the front of that report.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Krupa na Uni, Krupa on the Una river, just as we saw that Bosanski Petrovac dropped the "Bosanski", similarly here, Krupa is dropping the Bosnian identification and calling itself simply the Krupa on the Una.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a long document.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on page 5 in the translation, the last two paragraphs on that page, and I will look for the -- there it is. The B/C/S is page 4 of the B/C/S, that is, 00552818. It mentions that -- in discussing the work of the Crisis Staff, they discuss the Crisis Staff's involvement in the removal of Muslims. In the beginning of the third paragraph on page -- I'm sorry, in the middle of the third paragraph: "The War Presidency of the Serbian municipality offered the Muslims two options. They could organise themselves and, with our guarantees and full protection, move out to the destination of their transfer, or this would be done by military means." In the next -- beginning of the next paragraph, they explain that: "The reason for adopting this decision on the temporary transfer was the physical safety of the Muslim people and the historically proved and confirmed nobility and kindness of Serbs who do not have a propensity for crimes and genocide."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you for a comment regarding --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to that, of course it's necessary to avoid reading out all sorts of superfluous context, but from the English translation, what Ms. Hanson read out here in open court started in the middle of a sentence, and really, in this particular case, I do suggest that the whole sentence should have been read out and should now be read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please indicate where you'd like Ms. Hanson to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The words "the weak response" in the translation, which is almost halfway down that penultimate paragraph on page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You wish me to read that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The weak response or total disregard of Muslims to the call for surrender of arms, and Alija's threat that Krupa must become green whatever the cost, forced the War Presidency of the Serbian municipality to offer the Muslims two options: They could organise themselves and, with our guarantees and full protection, move out to the destination of their transfer; or this would be done by military means."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave that one, the second statement you read to us made a reference to the temporary nature of the removal. Can you comment on that what regard to what Miroslav Vjestica from Krupa had to say in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said to the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May that he -- having heard the happy news of where the borders will be set, he does not think that there will be a place for Muslims to return to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I would like to show you presentation tab 223, master tab number 342. This is also from Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order of the War Presidency of Bosanska Krupa, dated the 22nd of May, 1992, an order to evacuate the remaining Muslim population from the territory of Bosanska Krupa, and, again, tasking the public security station and the military police to implement this order on evacuation. And the evacuation should be directed towards Cazin Krajina. Cazin Krajina was an area of Bosnia held by -- not claimed by the Serbs, so Bosnian Muslim territory. I would note here, it says "the remaining population," those who've not yet left are to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours, at presentation tab 224, master tab 429.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an intercept, an intercepted telephone conversation from the 12th of May, 1992. And can you tell us who the speakers are and where we're beginning on both the English and B/C/S versions of the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speaker -- one speaker is identified as Nedeljko Prstojevic, as we've seen, commander of the Ilidza Crisis Staff. The others are an unidentified Milenko and then an unidentified Novakovic. I don't have any information on who they might be. The excerpt starts in the seventh box -- oh, no, I'm sorry, I don't -- the sixth -- fifth box from the bottom, Prstojevic saying, "Why did Mika phone me?" I'll find it in the B/C/S. It's at the top -- towards the top of the second page, 04013854, the sixth box from the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would note for the interpreters, as I recall, I think this is a pretty rapid conversation, and it's about two pages. We're ready to play it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Why did Mika phone me? Milenko: Milenko ... phoned you to check with you ... these people in Kotorac. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Yes. Milenko: What should we do with them? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Did you arrest them? What did you do. Milenko: People are down there on ... Just a second, one second ... (Milenko is telling people in the room to be quiet) Yes? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Hello? Milenko: Yes? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: And where are those people? Have they been arrested? Milenko: No. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: What then? Milenko: ... Down there on the road, all of them. Men are separated from women. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Ha ... Milenko: Just a second, just a second. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: ... Up there... right? Milenko: He says men ... I've just received the word: Men are in the Kula prison, and women went in the direction of Butmir. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Put Tepavcevic on. Milenko: Here, here's Novakovic. He will talk with you. It's Prstojevic, stop fooling around. NOVAKOVIC: Hello? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Hello? NOVAKOVIC: Hi, Nedja. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Hi. NOVAKOVIC: How are you? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: I'm fine. Have you been cleaning Kotorac today? NOVAKOVIC: They have. I don't know the exact details, because I was engaged otherwise. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Yes. NOVAKOVIC: Well, if you want we will call you later, well, while ... Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: That's ok, but tell me, please, I beg of you, why did you take women to Butmir? NOVAKOVIC: They said women were not in Butmir but ... Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: But? NOVAKOVIC: Well, in Butmir, yes. Not to KP Dom, but to Butmir. That's where they're going. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: They cannot go to Butmir, we'll mop up Butmir in time as well. NOVAKOVIC: Aha. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Butmir will be mopped up, Sokolovic will be mopped up, Hrasnica will be mopped up. NOVAKOVIC: Well, I don't know where to take them? Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: They will all ... There is Bascarsija. Please take all of them to Bascarsija, on foot. NOVAKOVIC: Aha, aha. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Women. NOVAKOVIC: OK, now I'll ... Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: And men to prison. NOVAKOVIC: OK. I'll check with them now and then I'll let you know. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Yes. Tell them, those who convert to Orthodox religion on the spot, they can stay, women and children. NOVAKOVIC: Aha. OK. OK, now I'll ... Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: Do it, please, but don't make mistakes ... You've done an excellent job, but it means that Butmir will be mopped up in time. Tell that to the people there. NOVAKOVIC: Yes, yes. OK. Nedeljko PRSTOJEVIC: There you go. Cheers. NOVAKOVIC: OK."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the word that is translated as mopped up here is cistiti, or cistite. And in terms of what he means, mopping up, his emphasis that women who convert to Orthodox religion can stay, men will go to prison; otherwise, the women go to Bascarsija, that is, the centre of Sarajevo, which was held by the Bosnian Muslims at this time, indicates that it's not just about military operations to my mind; that those who convert to the Orthodox religion can stay, is a striking statement. And that he's planning to -- he has intention to cleanse, clear, mop up, certain neighbourhoods and therefore does not want more Muslims sent there, I think, is indicative of an -- his planning for future operations in those regions, those areas, neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see some -- we've talked about a few examples of where the Muslims were being removed from individual municipalities. Did you see some examples where there was coordination between more than one municipality in this process?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you tab 225 in the presentation, master tab 343, and ask you what that is.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is called "Conclusions Adopted at a Subregional Meeting of Political Representatives of the Municipalities of Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa" is how Krupa is described here, "Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc," and sent to a Crisis Staff of the autonomous region of Banja Luka, the leadership of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, and the 1st Krajina Corps. It's dated the 7th of June, 1992. I would note in this context, particularly item 6, which is on the second page of the translation and also of the B/C/S. "That all seven municipalities here agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities." The paragraph goes on to note that if the ARK leadership fails to solve this issue, "our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I want to go on to another paragraph in your report, paragraph 62. You talk about how Crisis Staffs oversaw the removal of non-Serbs by establishing variously named committees or agencies, for example, Committee for Immigration, Travel Agency, Exchange Agency. Let me show you tab 226 in the presentation, master tab 325. This is from Kotor Varos. Tell us about this one, please.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is minutes of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos, dated the 14th of July, 1992. On the first page in both the English and B/C/S, under item 2, the War Presidency says that: "Activities relating to moving out the population failed to meet expectations. This task must be dealt with in a much more organised fashion. An agency has to be established to handle these matters." I've seen agencies, as you mentioned, various kinds of agencies, some dealing with the exchange of property of those leaving and others with larger issues of how to move out -- move the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll skip the next tab, 227. It's referred to in a footnote in her report, and go to presentation tab 228, master tab 350.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document from Sanski Most on the 2nd of July, 1992. Did the Crisis Staffs set any criteria before people would be allowed to depart?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw several decisions on the criteria for moving out. This is one such decision from Sanski Most, dated the 2nd of July, 1992. Under Article 1, it notes that families and people may leave voluntarily from Sanski Most if they give a statement to the appropriate municipal organ that they are permanently leaving, and that they are leaving their real property to Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- did you see similar requirements in some of the other municipalities for being allowed to depart, in particular an indication that the departure was permanent?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several such decisions specify the arrangements for the real estate and the permanency of that -- the disposing of the real estate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you next to tab 229 in the presentation, master tab 344. This is from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an information or statement based on the decision of the War Presidency, dated 31st of July, 1992, and the statement is regarding the conditions by which Muslims may move away voluntarily from the municipality. And they may do so if they either exchange -- sign a contract on the exchange of their property or leave their property to the state. Notable here, at the bottom -- the last sentence of the first item, that "property may be given to close relatives from mixed marriages." So Muslims may leave but they -- the implication here is that only those from mixed marriages can leave their property to relatives. Others have to either exchange it or give it to the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you next presentation tab 230, master tab 354 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask a question? Did you find some examples, Witness, where there was an exchange of real estate? You seem to suggest to us that people would accept to sell and to receive another building in exchange, or another apartment in exchange. Do you have examples showing that this in fact took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing such examples; however, I would -- in that respect, I'm always dependent upon the evidence we have, and such agreements might be kept by people -- the people involved. And because we have records of -- from the municipal side, such agreements may not have entered the municipal record. But in terms of the documents I examined for this, I do not recall seeing such agreements, but I do see many indications of agencies being set up for this exchange, of the municipal authorities apparently creating the possibility for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- if I may indicate, I believe in the trial so far, I think both from one or two viva voce witnesses and some of the 92 bis materials, we have had some of our crime-base witnesses speak to this particular issue. I can't point you to a specific point, Your Honour, but there is some evidence on that that may be of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If my recollection is right, it was one of the Pale witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he did talk about an exchange of property and what he got when he got to Sarajevo. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, I think you have before you the presentation tab 230 --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, minutes of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos, dated the 29th of July, 1992. Here, I would draw your attention to item number 7, that the War Presidency says that people "moving away should be informed that they are allowed to take with them no more than 300 Deutschemarks."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, with regard to this process, I want to ask you about tab number 231 in the presentation, master tab 355. This is from Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is instructions on the evacuation of refugees -- of the inhabitants and refugees from the local community of Arapusa. It's signed by a representative from Arapusa from the refugee committee and from the command of the battalion, dated the 1st of May, 1992. At the beginning of the instructions, they refer to the order of the war staff of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa, dated the 29th of April, 1992, by which the evacuation of the inhabitants and refugees from Bosanska Krupa is ordered. And it's showing that on the basis of that order, the local community has organised -- prepared a plan of evacuation. Arapusa, I would point out, was a predominantly Muslim settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next one, I think, we'll skip, 232. This is in Ms. Hanson's report in a footnote and pertains to payment of transportation for refugees from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 233 in the presentation, master tab 300. Ms. Hanson, this is from Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most, dated the 23rd of June, 1992. Here, I would draw your attention to what is listed as item (h) on the first page; in the B/C/S, I'm just checking where it -- oh, yes, it's (g) in the B/C/S. No, I'm sorry, I'm confused here. I'm sorry, it's at the bottom of the first page in the B/C/S, under Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. letter (e). The Cyrillic -- it's not -- anyway, I'm sorry, I'm confused. The sentence I want to read is that: "Nedeljko Rasula and Mladen Lukic are given the task of travelling to Prijedor to negotiate quantities of fuel for the use of Sanski Most municipality and at the same time to ask about the possibilities of the passage of a convoy of people who would like to travel by rail into Central Bosnia." Central Bosnia, at this time, I take that to be a reference to territory held by the Bosnian Muslim forces. And so we see that the Crisis Staff is talking to other municipalities about arranging passage -- arranging convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that takes us to the end of binder number 5. We're just -- I don't know if you want to take a break at the normal 10.30 time; in light of our late start, if you want to continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to take two breaks anyhow, so whether this would be a better moment or after the -- you've introduced your new subject. I'll leave it up to you. But somewhere within the next seven to eight minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask her a question to follow up on the topics we've just been talking about, and then I'll ask if we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, that just concludes our discussion of how the Crisis Staffs were involved in the removal of non-Serbs. In some of the documents we saw, and some that you referred to in your report, the municipality authorities and in some of the higher level authorities, they seemed to indicate that they're simply trying to help the non-Serbs who want to leave the area. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do see that. However, I have not seen references to Crisis Staffs discussing the possibility of moving those people to another safe part of the Serbian municipality or to another safe area of the Bosnian Serb territory. But the idea of safety seems to refer to moving them out of Serb territory altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see in some of the documents you reviewed for this where there were discussions, for example, in the municipality, in the Crisis Staff meetings, where local Muslims or other non-Serbs were requesting to be allowed to stay?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any examples in the documents where the local Muslims were requesting to be allowed to stay, even though there were wartime conditions and a lot of anti-non-Serb bias?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing any such requests of Muslims who wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the removal, whether it was temporary or permanent, did you see any evidence to suggest that it was not temporary?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw -- as we see, the decisions regarding property indicate that it's permanent. We do see -- we looked at briefly in the Krupa War Presidency, they say it was for their temporary removal, but we also have the comments of a member of that War Presidency that he does not expect the Muslims to return. We also see War Presidencies and Crisis Staffs deciding who can return and cannot, and taking -- making efforts to return Serbs but not making the same efforts to return non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to go into another area. Can we take a break at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break. We had a late start -- we'll resume at 10.55, five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The fact that the Chamber returned late gives no right to the parties. It's always because there are a lot of things to do during the breaks which sometimes take even more time than expected. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, we just finished talking about the removal of non-Serbs from the municipality, and discussed the issue about whether that was meant to be temporary or permanent. In your report, at paragraph 63, you talked about how the Crisis Staff oversaw the collection and redistribution of the property that had been left behind when the non-Serbs left or were forced to leave, and, in many cases, signed over their property. Binder tab 234 is a document we looked at before, which is from a Presidency decision, and I'll skip over that one, Your Honours, and go to 235, which is master tab 357, and, Ms. Hanson, ask you to direct us to the page in that document you want to talk about and what point it illustrates regarding ...

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is also a document we have seen before, the accounts of the Serbian municipality of Ilijas. But in this context, I would just turn you to the last page of the translation, the B/C/S page 02252626, where, after the summary, there are some remarks. And the first remark notes that some of the income came from goods taken by the Crisis Staff's order, from the shop of Mirsad Tokac -- I'm sorry, it does not say that it was part of the income. I was misunderstanding from the first page. But it says that goods were taken by order of the Crisis Staff from the man's shop to the Trgopromet company. So it's -- the name of the shop owner, Mirsad, is a typically Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there an estimated value of the property that was taken?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1.500.000 dinars, which is about -- I had the figure in my notes, I'm sorry, I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you had indicated it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $4.600 at the time.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just as an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to skip the next presentation 236, it's a document in the footnotes to her report, and go to tab 237, which is master tab number 430.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hannis, I have a question for the witness, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In document 235, I do not understand "for incomes." What was the status of the Snaga shop or supermarket manager, Ozren Hotel? Maybe this is rather naive question, but had these shops being requisitioned? Did they belong to someone? Were these shops then operated directly by the municipality of the commune? Can you give us some information about this. It's not the Crisis Staff who was directly operating or managing these establishments. Did they appoint someone to operate these establishments? Can you provide us some more information about this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no further information on these institutions in Ilijas. Ilijas is not a municipality for which we have very detailed reports, so I don't know whether this came as a tax on -- a sales tax, tax on income from these businesses, or whether these were businesses whose profits went directly to the municipality. I have no further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But, in other cases you've studied, was it customary for municipalities to directly manage, to directly operate goods or properties that, in the past, belonged to individuals? Do you have any other examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no examples of that, to my knowledge, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that in our upcoming witness schedule, I think we have two or three witnesses from Ilijas who will testify in a couple of weeks, so we may be able to address that issue at that time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Subject to the ruling on the application for an adjournment, Mr. Hannis means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's only for the weeks to come. But I take it that's somewhere in the presentation of the Prosecution case, and that's how I understood Mr. Hannis's remark. The timing is, I fully agree, totally in the hands of the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I'd like to go next to presentation tab 237, which is master tab 430. This is a document from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decision of the Crisis Staff, dated the 23rd of June, 1992, on -- instructing those who have -- citizens of the municipality who have left to report to the municipal secretariat for economy, urban planning and finance, by the 10th of July. If they fail to report, their property "shall be declared the property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipality of Prnjavor." I would note in this context that it's not a long time period from the date of the decision to the date by which they lose their right to the property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any indication in that document that the proceeds from that property would be held in trust in the event that the owners were to return after the conflict died down?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says it would be declared the property of the state and at the disposal of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you next presentation tab 238, master tab 364. This is a document from Kotor Varos, on the 28th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the minutes of the War Presidency. Under item 2 on the middle of the first page of the translation: "In relation to the report of the chief of the public security station on confiscating the money of individuals who are moving out, it was established that this was being done without anyone's order, i.e., in an unauthorised manner," and so it was decided that the money confiscated in this manner -- I'll finish the sentence. I was trying to summarise, not trying to leave out anything significant. "... this can have a negative effect on the operation and the reputation of all of us. It was decided that the money confiscated in this matter will be used to help the families of soldiers killed and other essential costs of the Municipality."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report, at paragraph 64, you indicate that that is a sign that the removal was meant to be permanent rather than temporary, that some Crisis Staffs took measures to ensure non-Serbs would not return. Let me show you presentation tab 239, master tab 367, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document on a conclusion of the war staff of Kalinovik, discussing a decision made on the 17th of May. It doesn't quite have the form of a regular conclusion, but it is signed and stamped. It's just that the date isn't in the usual place. Notable here, the second paragraph. The conclusion is regarding men of military age, of Muslim nationality, that they were to report to the secretariat for national defence between the 20th and the 25th of May; if they fail to report at this time, they shall be proclaimed opponents of the SOS, banned from returning to the municipality, and their property shall be confiscated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have two more documents related to this point. Presentation tab 240, master tab 368, this is from Kotor Varos Crisis Staff or War Presidency, on the 11th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of item 2, the last paragraph of item 2, the War Presidency wants to form a commission to make a selection of which -- to allow some refugees to return to their homes, but not others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mention any criteria which will be used for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't specify that here, but it's the War Presidency, apparently, who's setting up the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on this issue, let me show you presentation tab 241, master tab 366. This is from the Ilidza municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's titled "A Programme for the Return of Serbs from SR Yugoslavia," dated the 21st of June, 1992. Under item 4, at the bottom of page 1, this plan notes that -- if I could just see the ... It seems that the revised translation has not gotten into the binders. Could I read the B/C/S and have the interpreters translate the relevant passage?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I'm getting confused with these. Okay. [Interpretation] "From the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, not only the Muslim and Croatian population moved out or ran away, but also our own Serbian population. In order to have the Serbian population return, we kindly ask the government of the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina to adopt the following stances: 1, to take every possible step for the return of the displaced persons, refugeed Serbs." [In English] The emphasis in the original is that not only Muslims and Croats left Ilidza, but also "our Serbs," and the emphasis is on returning the Serbs from Yugoslavia. So the intention here of this municipality appears to be to make -- take efforts to return the Serbs, but not all who left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And no mention of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No mention of returning non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, that concludes the documents we wanted to show in the presentation related to your report. We talked in the beginning that you had prepared some case studies for three separate municipalities to sort of reflect the overall points you've been making. Before we move to that, was there anything you wanted to say to, sort of, sum up what we've talked about so far, before we do that, or do you want to go to the case study of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would direct the Court to my report. My written conclusions are perhaps more eloquent than I can say now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, those are contained in paragraphs 65 through 69 of her report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With that, then, Your Honours, I would like to talk about some of the case studies. First of all, would you tell us, briefly, how you chose those municipalities, and why you chose them, and what you intend to show with these case studies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to show what a good collection of Crisis Staff documents can tell us about the day-to-day operations of Crisis Staffs, and how they illustrate the themes which I've discussed. So I selected municipalities for which we have good, consistent documentary evidence, none of it, of course, perfect, 100 per cent complete. And many municipalities do not have such extensive collections. But that was one criterion. I also -- to show the extent of the pattern, I wanted a geographical distribution, so, according to those criteria, the best examples were Kljuc, Trnovo, and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just observe that -- I've just noticed that when there was a reference a few moments ago to paragraph 65 through 69 of Ms. Hanson's report, the numbering doesn't seem to fit. Of course, this is evidence in chief and I get to cross-examine, but I don't think the actual paragraph numbering fits what it was probably intended to say as a wrap-up of that bit of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also notice that somewhere in this range we jump to the conclusions, for example, if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But 69 doesn't fit either, because 69 is the second paragraph of the section dealing with conclusions, so I don't think it can have been intended to be 65 to 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have my report with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I misspoke. I was looking at an earlier version. I think I should have said paragraphs 68 through 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the conclusions, then. So Mr. Hannis was referring to your conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I, before you do so, Ms. Hanson, I do understand that there are municipalities where there is more documentation as to others. You used the words "pattern," which is, of course -- well, I would say, to establish a pattern is not always an easy matter. May I take it that, if -- from any of the less-documented municipalities, if there is documentation which would go against your conclusion of what would be your conclusion on the well-documented municipalities, you will draw our attention to that when dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we're talking about three municipalities. There were many municipalities, and, of course, if you say they are well-documented and this would allow us to establish, I would say, what would be a pattern in these three municipalities, and might be a pattern for the other municipalities as well on the condition that there are not contradictory elements in those documents pertaining to the other municipalities. Of course, I'm not asking for every detail. But if in one of the other municipalities, although less documented, if you find one, two, or three clear indications that it was different there, we would like to be informed about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To clarify my comments, when presenting these case studies, I'm not claiming that everything that happened in these municipalities happened elsewhere. I'm not taking them to stand for other municipalities. When I referred to a pattern, I meant the themes that I discuss in my report. When I discuss a theme, such as the military role or the question of detention centres, on one topic, I take from many municipalities, and so we've been jumping around with a lot of documents. What I wanted to do with the case studies was turn that study upside down and say, Here's one municipality; what, of the topics I've discussed, can we see there? So I'm saying here's what happened in Kljuc. I'm not trying to say that what happened in Kljuc happened in the same way in other municipalities, but rather, the themes that I've discussed, we can see all in one -- or a fairly finite set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. And you pointed in your report already to sometimes a pattern not being very clear, such as on the military matters, where you clearly indicated that it was different, depending on presence of the JNA, different on whether orders were given or received. So that's just for our understanding, that we know what you're talking about if you talk about a pattern.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To follow up on that, Ms. Hanson, I think you've made that point in your report, but we've also talked about this before, that you see wide variation with regard to many of the themes in the various municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've talked about some of the factors that influence that. Could you go through two or three of those for us again? I know one we talked about: Location.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did that affect?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how closely the municipality was located to areas of conflict, or how heavy the conflict was in that area; how close to the border of the Serbian territory as opposed to being in the centre; the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about timing.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The timing, as we saw, is -- what obtained in April is not necessarily the same situation as obtained in June. My report, as I note, is concentrated on that time period mostly, in terms of the most interesting events at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned before personalities.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personalities involved. Some personalities just had more interest in moving and shaking on the ground; some personalities had closer contacts to the centre because of personal ties and political -- long-standing political ties. So that can also be a factor. Also, the makeup of the population. We talk about variant A or variant B, but, of course, some were much more heavily Serb, with very few non-Serbs. Some had a closer balance of population. So those were all factors. I have to point out also, from my end, one variation is the amount of evidence available to me, and I cannot know what we don't have. I cannot know how much another municipality might have had documents that were not made -- never got to the Tribunal, so that can also influence my appearance of the pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asks you to take into consideration material you do not have. Only the fact that you have little information on certain municipalities should make you more cautious in drawing any conclusions. Well, I think the context of your case studies is thus established in such a way that we'd like to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to Kljuc, before I show you the first document, can you tell us briefly, what was the universe of documents from which you were able to draw on in respect of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a lot of minutes, handwritten I might note, of the SDS of Kljuc, as well as a book of minutes of the Crisis Staff of Kljuc. That book of minutes starts on the 27th of May, but prior to that we have other -- and subsequent to that, because I believe it ends at the end of June, we have other decisions of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency, and we have a handwritten diary of a member of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency. Kljuc is a municipality with quite good documentation overall, which is, as I said, one of the criterion for selection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me begin by handing you presentation tab 242, which is master tab 41, from the 23rd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the minutes of the meeting of the executive board of the SDS on the 23rd of December, 1991. We have seen this document briefly in the discussion of the implementation of the 19 December instructions. But just to take it a little more to see what the municipality was doing in reaction and how -- to these instructions, and how they discussed them. Kljuc was -- had a very close balance of Serbs and Muslims. The Serbs were a slight majority, just over 49 per cent, while the Muslims were, I believe, just over 47. So it was A, in terms of Serb majority, but a close balance. As we've seen before, under agenda item 1, briefing on the materials arrived from the Serbian Assembly. Veljko Kondic informed the meeting of the instructions for the organisation and activities of the Serbian people in BiH. "All organs will be required to act in accordance with the instructions. Whoever is not ready to fulfil its duties should say so immediately, and it will not be held against him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, we all are speaking more quickly when we read than when we have to invent the words at the very moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would note, then, further down on that page, which is in the B/C/S -- because these are handwritten Cyrillic, finding the B/C/S will always take me a moment longer. It's on page 00914529, in the middle of the page. The composition of the Crisis Staff is consistent with the 19 December instructions. It includes the deputy in the Assembly. The deputy from Kljuc was Rajko Kalabic, and we'll see that he speaks at this meeting. I would also note that Ljuban Bajic is named as secretary of the Crisis Staff. I note that because his diary is one of our exhibits. All the appointments that they named to the Crisis Staff are consistent with the 19 December instructions. And at the top of page 2 in the translation, still on the same page in the B/C/S, Rajko Kalabic informed those present on the issues considered in the second part of the Serbian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Assembly proceedings. There was a session of the Serbian Assembly on the 21st of December. So we see the channel of communication, the way -- as described in the Assembly sessions before, that the deputies convey information to the municipality. We see Kalabic doing that. On the same page in the translation, and the next page in the B/C/S, 00914530 -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm trying to avoid the highlighted section. Pardon me. One member asks that the meeting be informed about the second stage, and Kalabic said: "The first stage is the preparation for the second stage so there is no need to introduce the second stage," another reference consistent with the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question. If you say that "Rajko Kalabic informed those present on the issues considered in the second part of the Serbian Assembly proceedings" what is that exactly, the second part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original says -- yes, the second part. I'm just seeing where it says the "pauza". It says, if I read the B/C/S just to see if the order of words makes anything more clear. This is on 00914529. [Interpretation] "The second part of the Serbian Assembly, after the break, the presidents were informed by Kalabic Rajko." [In English] As to what they mean -- whether it means simply the part after the break -- whether the break was in the Assembly session that he's reporting on or in the -- this meeting here, it's not entirely clear.
